question: Write the differences between mitosis and meiosis?

To understand the functional relationship between these phases, Potu Narasimha Rao and Johnson (see annexure) conducted some experiments using the cell fusion technique. That is combining two cells in experimental conditions. With this cell fusion technique they revealed for the first time the structure of interphase (G1, S and G2) chromosomes that are not ordinarily visible under the microscope. They provided evidence on progression of cells through the cell cycle in sequential unidirectional and controlled way by a series of chemical signals that can diffuse freely between nucleus and cytoplasm. These experiments are considered to be a ‘mile stone’ in the cell cycle studies. (Fig-29) The division of nucleus (Karyokinesis) followed by the division of Cytoplasm (Cytokinesis) finally brings about formation of two daughter cells. While observing cells in tissues undergoing division, it is not easy to differentiate different stages of division. see table-1. 144 Reproduction Table-1: Mitosis 6.14.1 Meiosis Unlike mitosis which is a continuous process for division in most of the cells. Meiosis occurs only during the formation of gametes in sexual reproduction. Meiosis has two phases. During the first phase of meiosis the parent cell containing two sets of chromosomes (diploid) divides and daughter cells containg one set of chromosomes (haploid) are formed. The second phase of meiosis is similar to normal mitosis. Thus the four daughter cells have just half the number of chromosomes of the parent cell. Stage Description 1. Prophase 1. Chromosomes condense and get coiled. They become visible even in light microscope and nucleoli become smaller. 2. Chromosomes split lengthwise to form chromatids, connected by centromeres. 3. Nuclear membrane disappears. 4. Centrosome, containing rod-like centrioles, divide and form ends of spindle (probably animal cells only). (Note: No pairing of chromosomes as in meiosis). 2. Metaphase 1. Chromosomes move to cell equator, spindle fibres attached to centromeres. 3. Anaphase 1. Centromeres split, separating the chromatids. 2. Spindle fibres attached to centromeres contract, pulling chromatids towards poles 4. Telophase 1. Chromatids elongate, become invisible, replication at this stage to become chromosomes. 2. Nuclear membranes form round daughter nuclei. 3. Necleolus is resynthesized in each daughter nucleus. Cytokinesis 1. Nucleus divides into two and division of cytoplasm starts Two cells are formed. 2. Therefore, many ways have been devised to avoid pregnancy. The chemical nature of the genetic material was determined after a series of experiments over the next 50 years, culminating in the determination of its structure the deoxy ribonucleic acid (DNA) in 1953 by James Watson(DNA) and Francis Crick. Scientists proved that mitosis takes place in all body cells which retains same number of chromosomes. Meiotic division takes place in sex cells where the chromosome number is halved. Observe the Fig-27. 6.13 Cell division in Human beings We know that cell is the structural and functional unit of life in all organisms. Cell division is a life process. The process of cell division is same in unicellular organisms and highly evolved multicellular organisms like human being. In all organisms the cell divide and form new cells. Cell division is the process that transforms a human fertilized egg into a baby in 9 months and into an adult in the next 20 years. Cell division and function in a multicellular organism is highly regulated. It occurs only when there is a need for it. Fig-27: Cell division showing mitosis and meiosis bone muscle skin nerve gland blood other cells sperm egg Zygote (fertilised egg) sperm egg immature reproductive cell Two kinds of cell divisions in the life of an individual. The chromosome numbers 2n and n are respectively the number of chromosomes following mitosis (2n) and half the number (n) following meiosis - the type of division predicted by Weismann. meiosis mitosis 142 Reproduction Cells in some organs, such as heart and brain of an individual may divide slowly. On the other hand bone marrow cells may actively divide to produce red blood cells, which have a short life span nearly 120 days in the body. For example, if you cut your finger and bleed, soon a blood clot forms to stop the bleeding. This brings in various chemicals to the site that stimulate skin cells to divide and heal the wound. Cell division ceases as the wound is completely healed. In contrast, cancer cells do not respond to such growth regulating factors and continuously divide at the expense of normal cells, thus ultimately killing the host. So it becomes important to understand the processes involved in cell division. The cell cycle will help us understand this better. 6.14 Cell cycle The process of cell division is a very small part of the cell cycle. It completes in 40-60 minutes. The period between two cell divisions is called ‘Interphase’. This is actually the period when the genetic material (DNA) makes its copy so that it is equally distributed to the daughter cells during mitosis. Interphase can be divided into three phases. 1) G1 phase: This is the linking period between the completion of mitosis and the beginning of DNA replication (Gap 1 phase). The cell size increases during this period. 2) S phase: This is the period of DNA synthesis (Synthesis phase) leading duplication of chromosomes. 3) G2 phase: This is the time between the end of DNA replication and the beginning of mitosis.(Gap 2 phase). When we say that something evolves, we mean not only that it changes, but that there is also some component of direction in that change. But, how does evolution take place?   "answer": "Mitosis and meiosis are two types of cell division, but they have several key differences. Mitosis is a process where a single cell divides into two identical daughter cells, while meiosis is a specialized type of cell division that produces four genetically diverse daughter cells, each with half the number of chromosomes of the parent cell. Here are the main differences between mitosis and meiosis:

1. **Purpose**: Mitosis is used for growth, repair, and asexual reproduction, while meiosis is used for sexual reproduction to produce gametes (sperm and eggs).

2. **Number of Divisions**: Mitosis involves one division, resulting in two daughter cells. Meiosis involves two divisions, resulting in four daughter cells.

3. **Chromosome Number**: In mitosis, the daughter cells have the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell. In meiosis, the daughter cells have half the number of chromosomes as the parent cell, which is why it is called 'reduction division'.

4. **Genetic Variation**: Mitosis produces genetically identical daughter cells. Meiosis produces genetically diverse daughter cells due to the process of crossing over and independent assortment of chromosomes.

5. **Phases**: Both mitosis and meiosis have similar phases (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, and cytokinesis), but meiosis has additional phases and more complex steps, such as the pairing of homologous chromosomes and the formation of tetrads.

6. **Occurrence**: Mitosis occurs in most body cells, while meiosis occurs only in the reproductive cells (gametes) of sexually reproducing organisms.

These differences are important because they ensure that organisms can grow, repair, and reproduce while maintaining genetic diversity.",
